canal-neyba-arroyo-rico-expropriations.title: Farmland and Cocoa Trees Taken Before Payment on Two Dominican Irrigation Works
canal-neyba-arroyo-rico-expropriations.place: The Canal Lateral Neyba between the Cuatrifurcación and El Sifón, Neyba and Duvergé, Bahoruco and Independencia provinces; the La Gina irrigation system with the Arroyo Rico and Río Jayán dikes, Miches, El Seibo province; and the Yuna-Cañabón system, Bonao, Monseñor Nouel province, Dominican Republic
canal-neyba-arroyo-rico-expropriations.point: Neyba, Bahoruco, the town the Canal Lateral Neyba is named after and one of the two municipalities the corrective resettlement plan names for that canal. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap. The plan for the Yuna-Cañabón works gives grid coordinates for its intake and canal tail, and the La Gina plan gives grid coordinates for the Arroyo Rico and Río Jayán dikes. No document found gives decimal degrees.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Emergency Recovery and Disaster Management Project (P109932), Loan 7546-DO, eighty million dollars, agreement dated 27 May 2008 between the Dominican Republic and the IBRD. The completion report of 22 April 2017 says the project was rated Category B and that "Two policies were triggered: Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Safety of Dams (OP/BP 4.37)"; it adds that the project did not expect to trigger either social safeguard policy and that only focal points for social safeguards were named in the implementing agencies. The evaluation review of 14 September 2017 gives the final list as Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Safety of Dams (OP/BP 4.37) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12). The Involuntary Resettlement policy was added at a level one restructuring, which the completion report dates to November 2010 and which both the review and the completion report's own restructuring table date to 1 October 2010. That restructuring covered only the activities of CDEEE, the state electricity corporation, which is the project's other implementing agency; it did not create a resettlement instrument for the irrigation works carried out by INDRHI. The evaluation review dates the approval of an additional financing of twenty million dollars, Loan 8098, to 17 November 2011; the completion report says its loan agreement was signed on 18 November 2011, that the loan was terminated when the effectiveness deadline of 17 August 2012 was missed, and that it was reinstated with the deadline extended to 16 November 2012. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, and so does the evaluation review; the review rates efficiency modest and efficacy substantial. The report says that in April 2014 it "appeared that INDRHI, which had limited knowledge of Bank Social Safeguards procedures, had begun expropriating farmers/private land owners in two locations in order to construct new canals/re-route existing canals", that "This situation occurred without the knowledge of the Bank and without the benefit of a project-level Resettlement Policy Framework in place", and that a Bank social specialist later "concluded that all persons who had been expropriated had received proper compensation". It says Resettlement Action Plans and Remedial Action Plans were prepared "although with important delays", were acceptable to the Bank, and that by closing the project was in compliance with OP 4.12. In its section on Bank performance the report says the Bank team "may have anticipated and prevented irregularities that occurred within INDRHI's activities" if the policy had been triggered project-wide in 2010, and that the team "took rapid action when INDRHI was found to be in non-compliance regarding the displacement of people, an element not covered at that time by a Bank pre-approved Resettlement Plan".

companies.name: Instituto Nacional de Recursos Hidráulicos (INDRHI)
companies.role: The Dominican state's water resources institute, which built and rehabilitated the irrigation systems and carried out the expropriations. Its Departamento de Derecho de Vía, the right-of-way department, valued the plots and trees and signed the agreements with owners, working with the project's own execution unit. The corrective plan for the Canal Neyba describes the institute's standing practice: "se procede a las firmas de los permisos y los trabajos se inician sin haber pagado las compensaciones correspondientes" — permits are signed and the works begin without the compensation having been paid. The plan also says the execution unit lacked a thorough knowledge of the Bank's OP 4.12.

companies.name: Hanson – Rodríguez, S.R.L.
companies.role: The firm contracted to supervise the Canal Neyba works. Its survey brigade measured the plots to be expropriated and identified the owners, and passed the figures to the project execution unit (corrective resettlement plans, 11 March 2016).

canal-neyba-arroyo-rico-expropriations.community:
Four corrective resettlement plans published on 11 March 2016 record what happened to farmers on two irrigation works in the Dominican Republic, and say they were written so that the project would be back in compliance with the World Bank's resettlement policy.

On the Canal Lateral Neyba, between the Cuatrifurcación and El Sifón, a new canal was built alongside the old one and a strip of farmland was taken from private plots. The plan for the next stretch of the canal says the expropriations on this stretch happened before the owners were paid: "Dichas expropiaciones ocurrieron, antes de otorgarles las indemnizaciones correspondientes a todos los propietarios de predios, localizados dentro del tramo del Canal Neyba Km 0.00 hasta Km 5.00." Thirteen plots are listed for the first five kilometres, all held without title. Every one carries 2 February 2014 as the date of expropriation. The first group of seven owners was owed 1,343,870 Dominican pesos; half was paid on 14 May 2014 and the rest on 17 July 2014, the plan saying the institution did not have enough money for a single payment. The second group of six owners was paid on 15 October 2014, eight months after the land was taken. The plots run from 0.15 to 24.31 tareas. The plan says no owner lost a whole plot, that nobody was displaced from the place, that no owner lost their means of support and that each lost only part of their fruit trees. It also says that before the land was taken the amounts had been negotiated and agreements signed with every owner authorising INDRHI to expropriate.

On the next stretch of the same canal, from kilometre 5.00 to kilometre 8.50, the plan says the owners were paid before their plots and crops were occupied, following the recommendations of a World Bank social safeguards mission. Its table lists thirteen cases paid on 9 April 2015 and expropriated on 4 May 2015.

On the La Gina system at Miches, in El Seibo, a strip of land was taken to make an access road for the heavy machinery working on the Arroyo Rico dike, and the crops standing on it were taken permanently. The plan says this happened before the owners were paid, and that the land itself was never paid for: "No se pagaron los Predios ocupados provisionalmente, en razón de que serán devueltos, una vez finalizado el Proyecto" — the plots taken provisionally were not paid for, because they are to be returned when the project ends. Only the fruit trees were compensated. Five cases are listed, all held without title, four expropriated on 10 September 2013 and paid on 28 October 2013, the fifth paid on 10 February 2015.

The same plan records two individual losses. Corrective action was taken for one affected person only, Isidro Peralta Amparo, after 63 cocoa trees were cleared on his land; he could not be reached for months because he lives outside the Dominican Republic, and was consulted and compensated once found. On the Río Jayán front, 63 cocoa trees were cleared to cut a bypass channel and the owner was paid on 16 March 2015. Another owner told the Bank's commission that he and the contractor had counted and agreed 75 cocoa trees, "pero sin embargo al final del proceso se cortaron ciento cincuenta (150) arboles Cacaotales" — in the end 150 cocoa trees were cut. The plan adds that apart from that occasion no further complaints were heard.

On the Yuna-Cañabón system at Bonao, six plots were taken permanently, all held without title, for a new intake and feeder canal. Three were paid on 26 December 2014 and expropriated on 8 January 2015; three were paid on 10 April 2015 and expropriated on 5 May 2015. One plot, held by two brothers, was outstanding and was settled on 28 December 2014.
canal-neyba-arroyo-rico-expropriations.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 128 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found counts people or households relocated. The corrective plans say the opposite: on the Canal Neyba "en ningún caso hubo necesidad de expropiaciones del total de predios, de desplazamiento del lugar" — in no case was a whole plot expropriated or anyone displaced from the place. The completion report puts it the other way in its section on Bank performance, where it says the Bank team took rapid action "when INDRHI was found to be in non-compliance regarding the displacement of people". The report and the plans are not reconciled by any document found. The counts the plans do give are of plots and owners: thirteen plots and thirteen owners on the first five kilometres of the Canal Neyba, thirteen cases on the next three and a half kilometres, five cases at La Gina and six at Bonao.
canal-neyba-arroyo-rico-expropriations.outcome: The completion report of 22 April 2017 says remedial action plans were prepared for the sites concerned with important delays, that a Bank social specialist concluded everyone expropriated had been properly compensated, and that by closing the project was in compliance with the resettlement policy. The La Gina plan says the land taken provisionally there was not paid for because it is to be returned at the end of the project; no document found records the return. The plan says INDRHI has nothing left to pay on that lot. The project closed on 31 October 2016, having been due to close on 31 December 2012.

canal-neyba-arroyo-rico-expropriations.confidence_note: Everything here comes from the World Bank's own documents: the completion report, the evaluation review of that report, and four corrective resettlement plans the borrower prepared and the Bank disclosed. No independent report was found. Searches of Dominican news and of INDRHI's own transparency pages for the Canal Neyba expropriations and for the Arroyo Rico works returned nothing on these events. Several figures are not reconciled by the documents. The completion report says the Bank acted on non-compliance "regarding the displacement of people" while the corrective plans say no one was displaced from the place. The plan for La Gina dates the World Bank social safeguards commission's field visit both to Thursday 11 December 2014 and to 9, 10 and 11 December 2015. The completion report dates the restructuring that triggered the resettlement policy to November 2010 while the evaluation review and the report's own restructuring table give 1 October 2010. The 63 cocoa trees cleared on Isidro Peralta Amparo's land and the 63 cocoa trees cleared on the Río Jayán front appear in two sections of the same plan; the plan does not say they are the same event, and neither figure is treated here as additional to the other. The dispute over 75 trees agreed against 150 cut rests on one owner's account as the plan reports it.

ceara-sanear-ii-resettlement.title: A Hundred and Fourteen Families Resettled for Water and Sewerage Works a Project Said Would Move Nobody
ceara-sanear-ii-resettlement.place: Fortaleza and the interior of the state of Ceará, Brazil
ceara-sanear-ii-resettlement.point: Fortaleza, the city the completion report names alongside "the interior of the state". Coordinates from OpenStreetMap. No document found names the neighbourhoods or the towns.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Ceará Inclusive Growth Project – SWAp II (P106765), Loan 7600-BR, lent to the State of Ceará with the Federative Republic of Brazil as guarantor, guarantee agreement dated 19 March 2009. The appraisal document of 29 August 2008 says "The SWAP II loan will continue supporting the 'Projeto Sanear II' to increase the number of water and sewerage connections in the state", that the operation draws on the resettlement safeguards framework already developed for that programme, and that "Only very limited involuntary resettlement is expected to occur under the water and sanitation component." The completion report of 18 December 2012 says "The project triggered OP/BP 4.01 (Environmental Assessment, Category B), OP/BP 4.10 (Indigenous Peoples), and OP/BP 4.12 (Involuntary Resettlement)", and that the resettlement policy was triggered "as a precaution" because the investments "were not expected to cause physical displacement of people". It rates the outcome Satisfactory and the risk to the development outcome Low or Negligible. The evaluation review of 15 May 2013 rates the outcome Satisfactory and the risk Negligible to Low, records no disagreement with the report on either, and says of safeguards "There have not been any issues."

lenders.name: Inter-American Development Bank
lenders.role: A partial financier of the state programme whose works caused the resettlement. The World Bank's appraisal document of 29 August 2008 describes the Projeto Sanear II as "a project that is partially supported by the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB)" and says the World Bank reviewed that programme's environmental framework and its resettlement framework and found both acceptable. No document found states the Inter-American Development Bank's loan number or amount for Sanear II.

companies.name: Companhia de Água e Esgoto do Ceará (CAGECE)
companies.role: The state water and sewerage company of Ceará, which carried out the water and sewerage works under the Sanear II programme. The appraisal document names it as the body applying the environmental and resettlement framework the World Bank reviewed.

ceara-sanear-ii-resettlement.community:
The World Bank's appraisal document for this loan said very limited involuntary resettlement was expected under the water and sanitation component, and the completion report of 18 December 2012 says the investments "focused on connecting existing households to water and sewerage networks" and "were not expected to cause physical displacement of people". The resettlement policy was triggered "as a precaution".

The same paragraph then records the outcome: "As it happened, however, the works required for the SANEAR II program led to the resettlement of 114 families in Fortaleza and the interior of the state." The report adds that "The appropriate framework, involving both consultation and compensation, was applied and the physical and symbolic impact of the resettlement was kept to a minimum", and that the Government of Ceará notified the World Bank before the actions were taken.

No document found names the places the families lived or moved to, says what they were paid, or reports how they fared afterwards.
ceara-sanear-ii-resettlement.displaced_label: 114 families resettled, per the World Bank completion report of 18 December 2012
ceara-sanear-ii-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 114 for this project. The completion report's figure is 114 families, not 114 people. ICIJ's table and the report's figure are the same number against different units, and no document found explains that. No conversion between families and people is made here.
ceara-sanear-ii-resettlement.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2012, on its original closing date. The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory and says the resettlement framework was applied with consultation and compensation. The evaluation review of 15 May 2013 says there were no safeguards issues. Neither document reports on the 114 families after the move.

ceara-sanear-ii-resettlement.confidence_note: The figure of 114 families rests on a single sentence in the World Bank's own completion report on its own project, and the evaluation review of that report does not mention it. No independent report was found; searches of Ceará news for the Sanear II resettlement returned only coverage of a later and unrelated desalination plant. The report gives no place beyond "Fortaleza and the interior of the state", no compensation figures and no follow-up, and says in the same sentences that consultation and compensation were applied and the impact kept to a minimum. The project's resettlement plan of 14 March 2008 does not carry the figure 114, so the number is not an appraisal estimate reprinted as a result.

skeldon-cattle-farmers-grazing-loss.drop_reason: Guyana Bagasse Cogeneration. Dropped by the checker on the lender link and on timing, not on the harm, which is real and well documented. The appraisal document of 25 January 2008 is the only outcome-side document for this number and it says three things that together break the link. First, what the Bank brought: "Apart from the CFU's support, the project does not include any World Bank or IFC financing" (para 23), the CFU support being a proposed purchase of up to 5.32 million dollars of emissions reductions by the Community Development Carbon Fund from the cogeneration plant, with the payment schedule still to be set "At the time of the signing of the Emission Reductions Purchase Agreement" — so no instrument was yet in force when the document was written. Second, what caused the harm: "Most of the adverse environmental impacts associated with this project are not the result of the bagasse cogeneration facility per se, but from the expansion of sugar cane cultivation under the SSMP" (para 49), the Skeldon Sugar Modernization Project, which the Bank did not finance; the safeguards table in the appraisal document is for the SSMP and is "presented here given the importance of the SSMP to the proposed cogeneration project". Third, when: the clearance and the impoundment had already happened. "Block 2 has now been cleared for sugar cultivation which means the Cattle Farmers Association is no longer able to freely graze their cattle there, and they have now been relocated to other Blocks"; "After many warnings, GuySuCo finally took the step of impounding 150 heads of cattle" (resettlement action plan of January 2008, annex 13, and appraisal document para 71). The appraisal document also frames the OP 4.12 case as moving cattle and not people: "While there is no involuntary resettlement of people in this project, there is a need to relocate the cattle that previously had grazed on Block 2 of the Skeldon Sugar Estate." No completion report, evaluation review or later plan for this number could be reached, so nothing records what happened at the Manarabisi pasture. The grazing block, the 150 impounded cattle and the 1,000 Guyana dollar fine per head are documented, but against GuySuCo's cane expansion before the Bank's carbon purchase, and the Bank's own document says the Bank financed neither. Keep the material: if a document is ever found showing the carbon purchase was conditional on the pasture works, or showing a lender for the SSMP, the row is a case against that lender.

rn34-colonia-santa-rosa-canteen-eviction.title: A Judge Ordered a Family Out of the Road Line Before the Colonia Santa Rosa Access Was Built
rn34-colonia-santa-rosa-canteen-eviction.place: National Route 34 near the junction with National Route 50, at the access to Colonia Santa Rosa, Argentina; the remedial action plan places the case in the province of Jujuy, near the Bolivian border, while the town of Colonia Santa Rosa is in the Orán department of Salta
rn34-colonia-santa-rosa-canteen-eviction.point: Colonia Santa Rosa, the place the remedial action plan names for this case. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap, which places it in the Orán department of Salta; the plan places the case in the province of Jujuy. No coordinates are given in any document found.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: National Highway Asset Management Project, second phase (P095569), Loan 7473-AR, four hundred million dollars, agreement dated 27 June 2008 with the Argentine Republic. The completion report of 28 March 2014 says the Involuntary Resettlement policy was not activated at appraisal because the works were expected to stay inside existing rights of way where no resettlement was expected, and that the policy had not been triggered on the first phase either. It then says that "activities under the project prompted the Bank to activate six safeguards policies, namely: The Natural Habitats (O.P 4.04), Forest (OP 4.36), Pest Management (OP 4.09) Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11), Indigenous People (OP 4.20) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.10)"; the last two numbers are the wrong way round against the Bank's own numbering, in which 4.10 is Indigenous Peoples and 4.12 Involuntary Resettlement, and the evaluation review of 5 November 2014 repeats the same list with the same numbers. The project was restructured in February 2012 to add the policies and the loan agreement was amended. The report says of those impacts that "The impacts were minor, however". The evaluation review says the land acquisition arose because "a few CREMA Contracts (or Mallas) required land acquisition because of temporary dislocation of settlement within the right of way", for roundabouts built as road safety improvements. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and so does the review. The review says "The ICR does not report on the compliance of these policies" and that the project team afterwards informed the evaluation group about compliance, which is a staff statement and not a document.

companies.name: Dirección Nacional de Vialidad (DNV)
companies.role: The national roads directorate of Argentina, inside the public works ministry, which ran the project and the CREMA rehabilitation and maintenance contracts. The remedial action plan lists the steps DNV was to take on each case, with deadlines, including obtaining the land and opening expropriation proceedings where owners would not agree. The completion report says it took DNV a while to grasp, internalise and accept what it calls the unexpected requirements from the Bank.

rn34-colonia-santa-rosa-canteen-eviction.community:
The remedial action plan filed under this loan on 7 December 2011 lists eight cases under the World Bank's involuntary resettlement policy where the project's road works had run into land the roads directorate did not own. In four of the eight the plan states that the works had already been carried out, one was dropped when the project was reformulated, two are marked for future relocation and one has no affected party listed.

The case with people in it is on National Route 34 near the junction with National Route 50, at the access road to Colonia Santa Rosa. The plan names a family that ran a comedor, a canteen, in the line of the road until 2009, and the owner of a depot who occupied the right of way. Its footnote sets out what happened: the canteen operator was served with judicial notice in 2002 that he was in the right of way, a judge ordered his eviction in 2009, and he moved to Saucelito with the support of the municipality. The plan says the works had already been done, and the step still owed to the World Bank was for the roads directorate to send a report from the municipality of Colonia Santa Rosa documenting the relocation of the family that ran the canteen and the measures taken to compensate or support the owner of the depot. A second footnote records that the depot owner is the widow of the man originally sued.

Two further cases on the same route, at the accesses to Embarcación and Aguaray, concern informal occupants of the right of way and a restaurant. The plan marks both for future relocation and requires an abbreviated resettlement plan to be sent to the Bank four months before construction of the access begins.

The other cases are land the works crossed without acquiring it from companies and a municipality: parcels of the oil company YPF at two places in Chubut, where the plan says the works had been done and the roads directorate was to obtain the land by agreement or begin expropriation proceedings, and land of a sugar company near the Calilegua National Park in Jujuy, where a new bridge and an access had been built and the works were still to be declared of public utility. One case in Jujuy was dropped when the works were reformulated.

A separate section covers the Bank's indigenous peoples policy: the rehabilitation and maintenance of a road in Neuquén affects the Namuncurá, Cayulef, Paineo and Cayupan communities, and the plan says those works had not yet been carried out and a plan for indigenous peoples existed in draft, based on a preliminary consultation with the affected communities.
rn34-colonia-santa-rosa-canteen-eviction.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 8 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document found counts the people moved. The remedial action plan of 7 December 2011 counts eight cases under the resettlement policy, of which one names a family that was evicted and had moved, and two more are marked for future relocation.
rn34-colonia-santa-rosa-canteen-eviction.outcome: The project closed on 30 September 2013, having been due to close on 31 December 2011. The completion report says the documents that are generally needed, a resettlement and remedial action plan and a framework for indigenous peoples, had now been drawn up during this project, and that the safeguards issue caused frustration among the roads directorate's staff and disruption to implementation. No document found says whether the municipality's report on the canteen family was ever sent, whether the depot owner was compensated, or whether the land at the other sites was acquired. The evaluation review says the completion report does not report on compliance with the six policies.

rn34-colonia-santa-rosa-canteen-eviction.confidence_note: The eviction and the works on land that had not been acquired come from one World Bank document, the remedial action plan of 7 December 2011, which reports the eviction in a footnote and names the people in a table. The court order it describes was not located; no independent report was found. The plan places the Colonia Santa Rosa case in the province of Jujuy, while OpenStreetMap places Colonia Santa Rosa in the Orán department of Salta, and the documents do not resolve that. The judicial notice of 2002 and the eviction order of 2009 both predate the plan, and the plan does not say which contract built the access or when, beyond recording that the works had already been done. The completion report calls the impacts that led the Bank to activate the six policies minor. The completion report and the evaluation review both give the resettlement policy the number OP 4.10 and the indigenous peoples policy OP 4.20; the Bank's own numbering has them the other way round.

honduras-road-rehabilitation-ii-land-tak.title: Three Households Resettled and Land Taken in Two Hundred and One Cases on Honduras’s Second Road Credit
honduras-road-rehabilitation-ii-land-tak.place: The San Lorenzo–Olanchito, El Porvenir–Marale and La Esperanza–Camasca roads and the El Porvenir by-pass, Honduras
honduras-road-rehabilitation-ii-land-tak.point: La Esperanza, Intibucá, the start of the La Esperanza–Camasca road, which carries 109 of the 201 cases the completion report counts. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap. The completion report names the road corridors and gives no coordinates, and does not say which corridor the three resettled households were on; the project’s resettlement plan of April 2008 places the only households it foresees moving on the San Lorenzo–Olanchito road, at the hamlet of La Tejera.

lenders.name: International Development Association (World Bank)
lenders.role: Second Road Rehabilitation and Improvement Project, filed as Honduras Road Rehabilitation and Improvement II (P109058), Credit 4466-HN, 29,600,000 Special Drawing Rights, financing agreement with the Republic of Honduras dated 13 October 2008, with an additional financing, Credit 4583-HN, of 16,800,000 Special Drawing Rights dated 2 August 2010. The completion report of 25 November 2015 says in its social safeguards paragraph that "The Project triggered the Bank safeguard policies OP 4.12 for Involuntary Resettlement and OP 4.10 for Indigenous Peoples", that an abbreviated involuntary resettlement plan and an indigenous peoples plan were prepared and disclosed, and that resettlement action plans were prepared and implemented for each road corridor to which they applied. It says that "During implementation, only minor issues were encountered such as administrative delays in the payment of compensation to affected parties." It rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and Bank performance Satisfactory. No evaluation review of this report was harvested.

lenders.name: Central American Bank for Economic Integration (BCIE)
lenders.role: Co-financier of the road works. The completion report of 25 November 2015 gives the project an estimated total cost of 64.6 million dollars, of which 48.6 million from IDA Credit 4466 "together with co-financing of US$15 million from the Central American Bank for Economic Integration (BCIE) and GOH financing of $1 million", and puts 14 million of the BCIE money into Component 1, the rehabilitation and improvement of the roads on which the land was taken, and 1 million into implementation support. A footnote to the report’s financing annex says BCIE "increased credit amount to US$22 mn based on revised estimated costs of La Esperanza – Camasca construction". The report does not say which credit paid for the works on any one corridor.

companies.name: Secretaría de Infraestructura y Servicios Públicos (INSEP)
companies.role: The Honduran public works ministry that ran the project and managed the right of way; the completion report also calls it SOPTRAVI, the name of the ministry when the project began. The report says social management capacity inside it went from effectively none at the start of the project to three full-time specialists at completion, and that the main focus was managing the right of way and building a more proactive capacity on land acquisition and resettlement.

honduras-road-rehabilitation-ii-land-tak.community:
The completion report of 25 November 2015 counts the land taken for the road works. Its sentence runs: the preparation and execution of resettlement plans for all the road improvements "was effectively carried, with the total number of cases identified and resolved with compensation effected in full as follows: San Lorenzo – Olanchito 8 cases; El Porvenir – Marale 25 cases (plus 59 cases related to the acquisition of land for the construction of the El Porvenir by-pass); La Esperanza - Camasca 109 cases (some additions possible given the works have not yet been completed). In 3 cases, households were resettled in all other cases compensation was paid in an aggregate total amount of US$0.45 million."

So three households were moved and the rest of the 201 cases were settled with money, 450,000 dollars between them. The report says compensation was effected in full, and that more cases on the La Esperanza to Camasca road were possible because the works were not finished when the report was written.

On how the payments were made, the report's safeguards section says that during implementation "only minor issues were encountered such as administrative delays in the payment of compensation to affected parties". It gives no count of the people affected by those delays and no length for them.
honduras-road-rehabilitation-ii-land-tak.displaced_label: 3 households resettled, per the World Bank completion report of 25 November 2015
honduras-road-rehabilitation-ii-land-tak.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's figure is 3 households. ICIJ's table and the report's figure are the same number against different units, and no document found explains that. The report's other counts, 8 plus 25 plus 59 plus 109 cases, are cases of land acquisition and compensation, not of people moved. The figure 3 also sits in the project's resettlement plan of April 2008, seven years earlier, as a forecast: "En el tramo de San Lorenzo – Olanchito, se prevé el reasentamiento de 3 familias" — on the San Lorenzo–Olanchito stretch the resettlement of 3 families is foreseen. That plan then records that only two of the three agreed to move, to the hamlet of Santa Bárbara a kilometre and a half away, and that the third, an 88-year-old woman represented by her daughter, asked for cash instead of being resettled. The completion report's sentence is in the past tense, "In 3 cases, households were resettled", and no document found reconciles it with the plan's forecast of 3 or with the plan's account of the third household.
honduras-road-rehabilitation-ii-land-tak.outcome: The project closed on 31 May 2015, having been due to close on 30 June 2013. The completion report says all 201 cases were identified and resolved with compensation effected in full, and that the works on the La Esperanza to Camasca road were not yet complete, so more cases were possible. No document found reports on the three resettled households after the move, or on how long the payment delays lasted.
honduras-road-rehabilitation-ii-land-tak.ecosystem: The completion report records that the planned road improvements ran up against the Refugio de Vida Silvestre Colibrí Esmeralda, a wildlife refuge found to be too small to sustain a viable population of the emerald hummingbird. Measures to enlarge the area and secure its management, with 1.8 million dollars in grant funding mobilised in 2009 through the Spanish debt buy-back programme, had to be completed before funds could be disbursed for the road works, and safeguards for endemic species were built into the design of the road itself. The Bank lifted the disbursement condition in March 2012.

honduras-road-rehabilitation-ii-land-tak.confidence_note: The counts and the payment delays come from one World Bank document, the completion report on the Bank's own project. No evaluation review of it was harvested and no independent report was found; searches of Honduran news and of the national audit office's published reports for the right of way on these three roads returned nothing on them. peru-rural-electrification-right-of-way-.title: Sixteen Per Cent of the Residents Owed Right-of-Way Payments Were Still Unpaid When Peru’s Rural Electrification Loan Closed
peru-rural-electrification-right-of-way-.place: Rural sub-project areas of the Electrocentro and Hidrandina distribution companies, Peru; no document found names the places where the right-of-way payments were owed
peru-rural-electrification-right-of-way-.point: Lima, the seat of the Dirección General de Electrificación Rural of the Ministry of Energy and Mines, which signed the subsidy agreements with the distribution companies and reported how much of the right-of-way money was still owed a month after the loan closed. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap. This is not a site of the harm: no document found names the sub-projects or the places where the payments were owed, and the appraisal document says only that the Distriluz companies serve twelve departments.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Rural Electrification Project (P090116, filed with the Global Environment Facility grant as P090110), Loan 7366-PE, fifty million dollars, loan agreement with the Republic of Peru dated 19 July 2006, together with Global Environment Facility Trust Fund Grant 056023-PE, which was cancelled in September 2012 after the government chose auctions for renewable electricity instead of the Small Hydro Financing Facility the grant was to finance. The Project Performance Assessment Report of 30 June 2017 gives the count: "The project triggered four of the World Bank's safeguard policies: OP/BP 4.01 on Environmental Assessment; OP/BP 4.12 on Involuntary Resettlement; OP/BP 4.10 on Indigenous Peoples; and OP/BP4.37 on Safety of Dams", the dam policy becoming not applicable when the small hydro component was cancelled. The completion report of 26 December 2013 lists the same four and gives the indigenous peoples policy as "OP 4.20 being revised as OP4.10". The three documents rate the project differently and each must be read from itself: the completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the global environment outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory; the evaluation review of 17 June 2015 rates the outcome Satisfactory; the assessment report of 30 June 2017 rates the development outcome satisfactory and the risk to it negligible. The loan's closing date was extended by eighteen months in two steps, and the assessment report says the second extension was needed "to enable right-of-way payments before project closing".

companies.name: Electrocentro
companies.role: One of the four regional distribution companies in the state holding company Distriluz, named in the appraisal document of 7 February 2006 alongside Electronorte, Hidrandina and Electronoreste. The completion report and the assessment report both name it as one of two companies that fell behind in making right-of-way payments to residents.

companies.name: Hidrandina
companies.role: Another of the four Distriluz regional distribution companies. The completion report and the assessment report both name it as the other company that fell behind in making right-of-way payments. The completion report gives its economic rate of return for the grid extension component as a negative value, the lowest of the companies it lists.

companies.name: Dirección General de Electrificación Rural, Ministerio de Energía y Minas
companies.role: The rural electrification directorate inside Peru's energy and mines ministry, which signed the subsidy agreements with the distribution companies, prepared the procurement plan and supervised contracting, and which reported the state of the right-of-way payments after the project closed. Its Directorate of Competitive Funding ran the sub-project side.

peru-rural-electrification-right-of-way-.community:
The documents on this loan record two kinds of loss to people in the way of the rural power lines.

Two families were moved. The completion report of 26 December 2013 says that on involuntary resettlement "two cases of families being moved were reported and reviewed" and that the Bank's specialist concluded they had been handled in a satisfactory way. The assessment report of 30 June 2017 repeats it.

More people were owed money for rights of way across their land and had not been paid when the loan closed. The subsidy agreements made the distribution companies responsible for meeting the safeguard requirements. The assessment report says two of the nine companies, Electrocentro and Hidrandina, fell behind. Both the completion report and the assessment report give the position afterwards. The completion report: "DFC-DGER reported that 86 percent of the amount of the right of way payments corresponding to 84 percent of the affected people had been made by July 31, 2013." The assessment report: "By July 31, 2013 (one month after the closing date), DFC-DGER reported that 86 percent of the amount of right-or-way payments, which corresponded to 84 percent of the concerned residents, had been made." So 16 per cent of the residents owed money had not received it a month after the loan closed.

The assessment report sets out why. The contracts with the installation companies did not say clearly who was responsible for the payments or how they were to be arranged. It adds three further obstacles: the absence of land titles, difficulty in locating landowners, and those owners' view that the amount they were owed was not worth the time and expense of cashing it. The completion report attributes the problem in part to the involuntary resettlement framework giving inadequate emphasis to right-of-way payments. It also records the lesson drawn, that right-of-way payments and compensation for the negative impacts of construction should be inside the project cost and written into the contractors' activities.
peru-rural-electrification-right-of-way-.displaced_label: 2 families moved, per the World Bank completion report of 26 December 2013 and the Project Performance Assessment Report of 30 June 2017
peru-rural-electrification-right-of-way-.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The documents' figure is 2 families. ICIJ's table and the documents' figure are the same number against different units, and no document found explains that. The proportion of residents still owed right-of-way payments is given only as a percentage; no document found states how many residents were owed money.
peru-rural-electrification-right-of-way-.outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2013, having been due to close on 31 December 2011. A month after closing the rural electrification directorate reported that 86 per cent of the money owed for rights of way, covering 84 per cent of the residents concerned, had been paid; the completion report and the assessment report both carry that report. The evaluation review of 17 June 2015 says the problems were resolved soon after closure. No document found says when or whether the rest was paid.

peru-rural-electrification-right-of-way-.confidence_note: All three sources are the World Bank's: its completion report, the evaluation group's review of that report, and the evaluation group's own field-based assessment report of 30 June 2017, which is the only one of the three that visited the project. The 86 and 84 per cent figures appear in both the completion report and the assessment report, in almost the same words. No independent report was found. Three figures for the same problem do not agree and the documents do not reconcile them: the completion report says "two distribution companies were late in organizing and completing these payments", the assessment report says "Two of the nine companies, however, fell behind in making such payments (Electrocentro and Hidrandina)", and the evaluation review says the issues were resolved "except for right-of-way payments for three sub-projects, which were resolved soon after closure". The two families moved are reported in one sentence in each of two documents, with no place, no date and no compensation figure.

colombia-water-easements-unsettled-at-cl.title: Twenty-Three Land Parcels and Eighty-Four Easements Were Still Unsettled When Colombia's Water Loan Closed
colombia-water-easements-unsettled-at-cl.place: Water and sanitation sub-projects in municipalities across Colombia, with two families awaiting resettlement in the municipality of Neiva, Huila
colombia-water-easements-unsettled-at-cl.point: Neiva, Huila, the one municipality the completion report names for an unfinished resettlement. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap. The report does not name the municipalities holding the 23 parcels or the 84 easements.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Water and Sanitation Sector Support Project, first phase of an adaptable programme loan (P082973), Loan 7281-CO, seventy million dollars, loan agreement with the Republic of Colombia dated 2 June 2005. The evaluation review of 18 September 2013 says the project was Category B and, "according to the POAD, triggered four safeguards policies: Environmental Assessment (OP 4.01), Cultural Property (OP 4.11), Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.12), and Indigenous Peoples (OP 4.10)". The three Bank documents disagree on the outcome and each rating is taken from the document that gave it: the completion report of 30 March 2012 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the evaluation review's ratings table gives Moderately Satisfactory for both the report and the evaluation group, with no disagreement recorded; the Project Performance Assessment Report of 29 December 2016, a joint assessment of three Colombian water projects, rates this project's overall outcome moderately unsatisfactory and the risk to the development outcome substantial. The review says an important cause of delay was "the difficulty in obtaining right of way permits (for easements), acquire land, and implement resettlement in accordance with social safeguards", and that sub-projects expected to take 16 months took 44 on average, the project closing 23 months late.

companies.name: Ministerio de Ambiente, Vivienda y Desarrollo Territorial
companies.role: The Colombian environment, housing and territorial development ministry, which ran the project through its vice-ministry for water and sanitation, hired three extra social specialists to work with the sub-projects and to draw up and supervise the remedial action plans, and was overseeing the unresolved parcels and easements directly at closing. In its comments on the completion report the ministry said the involuntary resettlement policy framework prepared for the project was unclear, and that completing the requirements in the remaining sub-projects "had a high cost for the nation".

companies.name: Fondo Financiero de Proyectos de Desarrollo (FONADE)
companies.role: The Colombian state development project financing agency, which administered the sub-projects. The evaluation review says provisions were made by FONADE for compliance with the safeguard policies, and that its capacity was weaker than the ministry's.

colombia-water-easements-unsettled-at-cl.community:
This loan paid for water and sewerage works in municipalities across Colombia, chosen through an application window that 550 municipalities applied to. Getting the land and the rights of way for the pipes was the problem the project did not plan for. The evaluation review of 18 September 2013 says land acquisition and easement issues "are commonly encountered in water supply and sanitation projects. However, they were not adequately factored into project design."

The mid-term review found what the completion report of 30 March 2012 calls "substantive and procedural issues in the application of involuntary resettlement and indigenous peoples policies". The ministry hired three social specialists to carry out field evaluations and to design a remedial action plan for each sub-project that needed one. An overall social remediation plan was approved on 28 April 2010, five years into a project that closed in March 2011.

The completion report gives the position at closing. A Bank review showed the ministry had completed 80 of 103 parcels and 1,093 of 1,177 easements satisfactorily. The remainder was unfinished: "The SRAP, however, is not complete as the resettlement of two families in the Municipality of Neiva and the legalization of 23 parcels and 84 easements are currently in progress." The report adds that full conformity was not realistic in the short term because most of the parcel and easement cases were caught up in legal and administrative procedures, and that the Bank would keep supervising the borrower's progress. The evaluation review puts the same facts as compensation: "At project closure in March 2011, compensation issues related to the legalization of 23 land parcels and 84 easements were still unresolved."

The ministry's own comments in the completion report say the involuntary resettlement policy framework prepared for the project was unclear, and that although it was committed to completing the requirements in the remaining sub-projects, doing so "had a high cost for the nation".
colombia-water-easements-unsettled-at-cl.displaced_note: ICIJ gives no displacement estimate for this project. No document found counts people or households relocated. The counts are of land: 23 parcels and 84 easements unsettled at closing, out of 103 parcels and 1,177 easements, and two families in the municipality of Neiva whose resettlement the completion report says was in progress rather than done.
colombia-water-easements-unsettled-at-cl.outcome: The project closed on 31 March 2011, having been due to close on 30 April 2009. At closing 23 parcels and 84 easements were unsettled and two families in Neiva were still to be resettled, and the completion report says most of those cases were caught up in legal and administrative procedures. The Project Performance Assessment Report of 29 December 2016, five years later, repeats the figures of 80 of 103 parcels and 1,093 of 1,177 easements completed satisfactorily and does not say what became of the rest, the two families in Neiva or the unsettled cases. It rates this project's outcome moderately unsatisfactory, against the moderately satisfactory of the completion report and of the evaluation review.

colombia-water-easements-unsettled-at-cl.confidence_note: All three sources are the World Bank's own: the completion report, the evaluation group's review of it, and the evaluation group's joint assessment report on three Colombian water projects, whose chapter 4 covers this loan. No independent report was found; a search of Colombian government and news sources for the unfinished resettlement in Neiva returned nothing on it. The figures of 23 parcels and 84 easements are counts of land, not of people, and no document found says who held them, what they were owed or whether they were ever paid. The two families in Neiva are named only by their municipality, and the completion report says their resettlement was in progress, not that it had happened. The assessment report, which is the only field-based document of the three, does not mention the unresolved cases at all, and the figures of 80 of 103 parcels and 1,093 of 1,177 easements that it does repeat come from a Bank review and a safeguards report by the ministry that the completion report says are in the project files and that were not located.

pelotas-street-vendors-shopping-popular.drop_reason: Brazil Rio Grande do Sul Integrated Municipal Development Program, Pelotas. Dropped by the checker on the figure and on the absence of any recorded loss. The figure first. The 500 is not a count of people removed and it is a plan reprint. The appraisal document of 10 December 2007 sets the intermediate outcome target for Component 2 at "500 cluster firms and street vendors, 200 rural producers" receiving training or technical assistance, with the year-five cumulative column reading 500. The completion report of 30 June 2014 reports the actual against that same row as "500 (street vendors); 60 (rural producers); 0; 0" and marks it "TARGET SUBSTANTIALLY MET", and the only sentence in the report that attaches the number to the facility calls them beneficiaries: "Results refer to the 500 beneficiaries of the Street vendors’ facility (Shopping Popular). At the start of the investment 50% of them ran formal businesses." No document found attaches a relocation verb to 500. The numbers that do carry a removal verb are in the report’s results annex and do not agree with 500 or with each other: "383 peddlers and 217 walking vendors benefited. 100 of the 600 persons targeted were not removed to the Shopping Popular since they had several stalls or changed their routes." 383 plus 217 is 600, which is the figure the same sentence calls the target. Turning 600 minus 100 into 500 is arithmetic the report does not do. Now the harm. The sentence the card rested on carries no count: "Rehabilitation of the urban city center led to the relocation of street and walking vendors to units within the Shopping Popular and other designated areas constructed as part of the Project. This was appropriately conducted, in accordance with Involuntary Resettlement Plans developed and implemented with the support and follow-up of the Bank." The completion report, the evaluation review of 22 June 2016, the loan agreement and the programme’s four resettlement framework documents were searched for a loss: grievance, complaint, protest, resistance, coercion, eviction. There is none. The report records the opposite on every point a loss could be read from: formality among the vendors rose from 50 to 70 per cent, the rent "was calculated to be sufficient to assure the maintenance of the equipment and at the same time the viability of the businesses of the beneficiaries", the municipality "has satisfactorily relocated street vendors to appropriate commercial facilities, not only improving their businesses", and the borrower’s own section says the building "allowed all walking and street vendors to move off of the streets". The four resettlement documents for the programme are the state-level Marco Conceitual da Política de Reassentamento Involuntário and an environmental and social management plan; none of them carries a Pelotas vendor census or count. That leaves the one source outside the lender, a preliminary conference paper by two Federal University of Pelotas researchers, which reports public demonstrations, a crisis around 2010 and the vendors accusing the authorities of "intransigência e coercitividade", and which gives no count of vendors, no income figure and no documented loss to any identified person. Accusations in a preliminary paper, with the lender’s own record uniformly recording improvement, is thinner than the standing edge of limb (b), and a relocation with no recorded loss on top of it is not limb (a). Two further notes for whoever revisits this. The paper’s URL, https://cti.ufpel.edu.br/siepe/arquivos/2013/CH_02959.pdf, answers 403 to a plain client from a web application firewall and opens through a browser route, so it is citable but not machine-fetchable. And the tightening of "policies of urban control in order to prevent the influx of new street vendors in central public areas" is the one line in the Bank record that describes a restriction rather than a benefit; it has no count, no enforcement record and no identified person attached, and a Brazilian municipal source on that policy would be the thing that makes this a case.

dennery-embankment-land-used-without-com.title: A Dennery Family's Land Was Built On Without Consent and Only Their Coconut Trees Were Paid For
dennery-embankment-land-used-without-com.place: The north embankment of the Dennery River, Dennery Village, Saint Lucia
dennery-embankment-land-used-without-com.point: Dennery, the village on the east coast whose waterfront and river embankment the works protect. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap. The land acquisition report names the river, the bridge and the families and gives no coordinates.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD and IDA)
lenders.role: The land acquisition and involuntary resettlement report of 20 February 2007 is headed "LC Disaster Management Project II" and is filed in the World Bank's archive under Additional Financing to the Second St. Lucia Disaster Management Project (P111708), whose approval ICIJ's table records as 15 July 2008. The report says the land acquisition request comes from Component 1 of the project, "Physical Prevention and Mitigation Works", which includes the coastal and flood protection works for Dennery Village, and that the request for additional financing to extend the north embankment "triggers the Bank's Operational Policy 4.12, regarding involuntary resettlement". It says the extension requires 6,039 square metres to be acquired out of total lands of 19,895.77 square metres, that this land is privately owned, and that the government now needs to acquire 30 per cent of the lands so the contractor can proceed. The works that had already been built are the parent project's. A Government of Saint Lucia press release of 7 February 2005 says the government secured 7.5 million dollars from two World Bank agencies for the coastal and flood protection of Dennery Village under the Second St. Lucia Disaster Mitigation Project: an IBRD loan of 3.7 million dollars and an IDA credit of 3.8 million dollars, with bids invited under World Bank guidelines. No completion report and no evaluation review filed under the additional financing number could be reached, and no document found for it states a loan or credit number or an amount.

companies.name: Mirai Construction Company Limited
companies.role: The contractor for the Dennery Coastal Protection Phases 1 and 2, awarded at a contract price of 6,683,042.53 East Caribbean dollars. The report says those works began on 26 July 2005 and were completed in the first week of September 2006, and comprised a 415-metre buried revetment, offshore breakwaters, an armoured berm and landfill. The report also names a second contract, the Dennery River Trou a Leau Ravine Works, awarded to Hippolyte Equipment Services (HES) and completed on 30 July 2007. It does not say which of the two contracts built the length of embankment that crossed the family's land.

companies.name: Smith Warner International
companies.role: The consulting engineers, of Jamaica, who prepared the final design report of October 2003, whose contract was varied in February 2006 so they could carry out a topographical survey of the area, and who supervised the earlier works contract. The report says the portion of the design that needed the family's land was left out of the bill of quantities because of land acquisition issues, and that the ministry considered in hindsight that time would have been saved by better communication at that stage.

dennery-embankment-land-used-without-com.community:
On 17 February 2007 a World Bank safeguards specialist met three representatives of the property owners whose land was needed to extend the north embankment of the Dennery River. Seven subdivided plots were represented. The report of that meeting, dated 20 February 2007, records what the owners said about what had already been done to their land.

The owners said their land had been used without their consent or any consultation for transporting, storing and dumping materials, and that their trees had been cut down. One loss is larger than that: "an area belonging to the Biscette - Regis family was used for the construction of the existing embankment without consent or compensation; the only compensation paid was for some coconuts trees that were removed." The family's representative, who speaks for four subdivided plots straddling the land where the embankment already stands and the land still to be acquired, said they were never informed or consulted about the project's designs, and had understood that the embankment would run along the river's edge. The report says the participants also spoke of their sense of helplessness, there being no grievance mechanism and nobody responsible they could take their concerns to. Their first contact with the project's intention to build an embankment, the report says, "was when the trucks and heavy construction equipment passed through or near their property".

The report records a meeting held at the end of January 2007 at which, it says, the contractor explained what his company would do and "stated that the government would expropriate the necessary land with or without their consent".

The same owners are for the works. The report says the participants agreed that the project itself will benefit their properties and the well-being of their town, that they acknowledge the benefits and "are eager to see the works extended and completed as far in advance as possible before this year's June storms", and that they had suggestions drawn from living through Hurricane Debbie and other floods, among them more drains and regular clearing of the existing one, which keeps getting clogged with elephant grass.

The report says the land still to be taken is 6,039 of 19,895.77 square metres for a 180-metre extension, that the original designs of the north embankment were over 90 per cent complete, and that since the designs were drawn in 2002 the owners had put up fences and enclosures on the land to be regraded.
dennery-embankment-land-used-without-com.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 11 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No document found counts people or households moved, and the report describes land taken from plots rather than homes removed. Its counts are of land and plots: three representatives at the meeting, seven subdivided plots represented, four of them the Biscette and Regis branches of one family, and 6,039 square metres of 19,895.77 to be acquired.
dennery-embankment-land-used-without-com.outcome: No completion report, evaluation review or later plan filed under the additional financing number could be reached, so no document found says whether the Biscette-Regis family was ever paid for the land the existing embankment stands on, whether the 6,039 square metres were acquired, or whether the 180-metre extension was built. The report of 20 February 2007 says a notice of the land to be affected had been sent for publication and that a valuation of each acquired property would follow a survey, with a tribunal process available for concerns and claims.

US $7.5 Million for Dennery Waterfront Protection Project (Government of Saint Lucia press release)

dennery-embankment-land-used-without-com.confidence_note: The harm rests on one World Bank document, the land acquisition and involuntary resettlement report of 20 February 2007, and within it on what the owners told the Bank's safeguards specialist at a single meeting. No independent report was found; a search of Saint Lucian news and government sources for the Dennery embankment land returned only material on the project's financing and on later flood works. The Government of Saint Lucia's press release of 7 February 2005 corroborates the financing of the works, not the harm, and comes from the borrower. The embankment that was built across the family's land is the parent project's, the Second St. Lucia Disaster Management Project, not the additional financing under whose number the report is filed; the additional financing was approved in 2008, after the report, and the report was written to support the request for it. The report does not say which of the two works contracts built that length of embankment. No sum is given for what the family lost or for what was paid for the coconut trees.

dangriga-market-vendors-income-loss.title: Twenty Dangriga Market Vendors Were Moved Out for Twenty-Six Months and Lost a Quarter of Their Income
dangriga-market-vendors-income-loss.place: The Dangriga Municipal Market, Dangriga, Stann Creek District, Belize
dangriga-market-vendors-income-loss.point: Dangriga Town, Stann Creek District, the town whose municipal market was rebuilt. Coordinates from OpenStreetMap. The abbreviated action plan names the market, the slaughterhouse and the Cubanos area and gives no coordinates.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Belize Municipal Development Project (P111928), Loan 7958-BZ, fifteen million dollars, loan agreement dated 2 December 2010 with Belize. The evaluation review of 5 September 2017 gives the count: "Eight of the Bank's ten safeguard policies were triggered. They were Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP/BP 4.04), Forests (OP/BP 4.36), Physical Cultural Resources (OP/BP 4.11), Indigenous Peoples (OP/BP 4.10), Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), Projects in Disputed Areas (OP/BP 7.60) and Projects on International Waterways (OP/BP 7.50)." The completion report of 5 June 2017 gives the indigenous peoples policy the number OP/BP 4.11 in its social safeguards paragraph, which is the number of the physical cultural resources policy. Both documents rate the outcome Satisfactory; the report rates the risk to the development outcome Moderate and the review rates it Modest. The report says "Four sites required development of Resettlement Plans. All vendors were resettled and moved to more lucrative locations, or compensated", and rates compliance with the social safeguard policies Satisfactory. The review drops the last three words of that sentence and reports it as "all vendors were resettled and moved to more lucrative locations", and adds that "The Bank project team confirmed to IEG that compliance with all safeguards was achieved for all subprojects by the end of the project", which is a staff statement and not a document. Neither the report nor the review mentions the income loss that the project's own abbreviated action plan of 20 August 2014 records. The total cost of the market sub-project is given in that plan as 1,519,364.33 Belize dollars, of which 1,475,111.00 from the World Bank loan and 44,253.33, three per cent, from the Dangriga Town Council.

companies.name: Belize Social Investment Fund
companies.role: The statutory fund that ran the project through its Project Implementation Unit, carried out the two evaluations of the vendors' losses and prepared the abbreviated action plan. The plan says the first contractor's works contract was terminated prematurely in September 2013. Channel 5 Belize reported on 30 January 2014 that work stopped amid allegations of an incompetent contractor and corruption at the fund, and Amandala reported on 4 April 2014 that four fund employees were dismissed after the first contractor alleged extortion in September 2013, and that the employees denied the claims.

companies.name: Dangriga Town Council
companies.role: The town council, which sought the funding to expand the market, put up three per cent of the sub-project cost, housed the displaced cooked-food and meat vendors in the renovated slaughterhouse and paid their utilities there, and operates the one-stall-per-family policy that the plan says affects five families, who are to be compensated with temporary stalls beside the Cubanos area. The plan says the council agreed to meet 14,990.68 Belize dollars of utility costs and 24,530.00 in stall-fee arrears for all the temporarily relocated vendors.

companies.name: K & G Construction
companies.role: The first contractor on the market works, whose principal the plan names as Mr Smart and whom Amandala names as Kenard Smart. dangriga-market-vendors-income-loss.community:
To rebuild and extend the Dangriga municipal market, the main market building was emptied. The abbreviated action plan of 20 August 2014 says a joint decision was taken to vacate it during the works because heavy equipment was operating next to vendors and the buying public. Those moved out were the stall owners inside the market, those under the market awnings, those in the fish section and those between the market and the Cubanos area.

Then the works stopped. The plan says the first contractor's contract was terminated prematurely in September 2013 and the civil works did not resume until April 2014, a seven-month gap. A second evaluation was carried out with the vendors who had been moved, to see whether they were losing income because of the delay. Its result: "Initially, a total of twenty (20) vendors were temporarily relocated but this number was reduced to twelve (12) by July 2014 with the majority of them relocating to other locations of the municipality where they are more visible to the buying public. The results of the second evaluation are that on an average, the vendors were experiencing income losses of 25%." The plan's own table gives the length of relocation for those 20 as 26 months, and marks each of their losses moderate.

The first evaluation, reported in April 2011, had concluded that most of the stall owners who would be moved "would not be experiencing any major loss of income sources or means of livelihood".

On 30 January 2014, while the works were still stopped, Channel 5 Belize reported Mayor Gilbert Swaso saying that vendors had lost about 25 per cent of their income while the market was closed, and that the community had lost its market. The same report said the shortfall of about 450,000 Belize dollars needed to finish the market would be taken from a 1.5 million dollar allocation for road works in Dangriga's phase two, money the mayor said would otherwise have paved about 1.2 miles of streets that residents had chosen.

What the vendors received is set out in the plan. The cooked-food and meat vendors were housed inside the renovated slaughterhouse, with running water and electricity paid for by the town council. The fish, fruit and vegetable vendors got temporary stalls beside the slaughterhouse, with some protection from the weather but responsibility for the security of their own goods overnight. Those who had traded between the market and the Cubanos area went to a temporary site pending a permanent one under a second phase. The council agreed to cover 14,990.68 Belize dollars of utilities and 24,530.00 in stall-fee arrears for all the temporarily relocated vendors for July 2012 to September 2014. At its August 2014 meeting the project steering committee approved reimbursements of stall fees to four of the relocated vendors, 6,955.00 Belize dollars in all, for July 2012 to April 2014.

The parking lot, where a large number of vendors had put up make-shift stalls, was to be taken back and the vendors moved into a new extension holding at most 22 stalls, one per family. The plan says five families are affected by that policy and names them: Zepeda, Carillo, Segura, Arzu and Sho. In the same paragraph it says temporary stalls will be erected beside the Cubanos area for those parking-lot vendors "who will be compensated with one or more stalls lost as a result of the Town Council’s one stall per family policy", and its table values the loss of the four parking-lot stall owners it names at one stall each and the loss of the other sixteen in the parking lot at none. A census of all the stall owners found that 56 per cent were women, that 70 per cent were of Mestizo ancestry in a town about 75 per cent of whose people are Garifuna, that 70 per cent paid between 15 and 22 Belize dollars a week for their stalls, and that weekly earnings ranged from 300 to 1,000 dollars in the parking lot to 900 to 3,000 dollars under the awnings. Fourteen sets of consultations were held with the vendors between April 2011 and July 2014.
dangriga-market-vendors-income-loss.displaced_label: 20 market stall owners temporarily relocated, for 26 months, per the project's abbreviated action plan of 20 August 2014
dangriga-market-vendors-income-loss.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 40 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The plan's own figure is 20 vendors temporarily relocated, falling to 12 by July 2014 as most of those moved on to other parts of the town. The relocation was temporary and within Dangriga: nobody is recorded as having lost a home. The plan's table gives the length of the relocation as 26 months and lists the 20 by name across three groups: six under the awnings, four between the market and the Cubanos area and ten inside the market.
dangriga-market-vendors-income-loss.outcome: The renovated market opened on 23 October 2014, Channel 5 Belize reported, after works that began in June 2012, with 44 stalls. The report gives the cost as 1,843,419.67 Belize dollars, above budget, with the first contractor paid about 800,000 before work stopped and the second contract costing roughly a million more. It quotes Mayor Swaso saying the building still lacked modern amenities and that some defects would be rectified, and says a government minister apologised to Dangriga residents for the delays. The project itself closed on 30 November 2016. The World Bank's completion report of 5 June 2017 says "All vendors were resettled and moved to more lucrative locations, or compensated", and rates compliance with the social safeguard policies Satisfactory; neither it nor the evaluation review mentions the 25 per cent income loss the project's own action plan records.
