dangriga-market-vendors-income-loss.confidence_note: The 25 per cent income loss appears in two places eight months apart, but both trace to the same side. The project's own abbreviated action plan of 20 August 2014 reports it from an evaluation carried out jointly by the project implementation unit and the Dangriga Town Council. Channel 5 Belize reported it on 30 January 2014, while the works were still stopped, in the words of Mayor Gilbert Swaso: "The vendors continue to lose twenty-five percent of their income." Swaso heads the town council, which put up three per cent of the sub-project cost, paid the relocated vendors' utilities and was a party to the evaluation, so the press report is an independent publication of a figure the council itself produced rather than an independent measurement of it. What the Belizean press does corroborate independently is the harm around the figure: the works stopping in September 2013, the market staying shut, the change of contractor, the cost overrun and a government minister apologising to Dangriga residents for the delays. The plan itself names the twenty vendors, gives the length of their relocation as 26 months and marks each of their losses moderate. Two limits should be read with it. The relocation was temporary and within the town, and the first of the two evaluations, reported in April 2011, had concluded that most of those to be moved would not suffer a major loss of income or livelihood. The corruption and extortion allegations around the first contractor and the Social Investment Fund are allegations as the press reported them, not findings, and the employees concerned denied them. The two press reports differ on the first contractor: Amandala names him as Kenard Smart of K & G Construction and Channel 5 Belize as Kenard Smart of Corozal, and the plan names only "Mr. Smart". Amandala gives the second contract as 1,228,310.95 Belize dollars signed on 24 March 2014 while the plan gives the whole sub-project as 1,519,364.33 and Channel 5 Belize gives the final cost as about 1.84 million; the documents do not reconcile these.

amoya-river-two-houses-relocation-planne.drop_reason: Colombia Amoyá River Environmental Services. The only document harvested is the appraisal document of 10 May 2004, for a purchase of emissions reductions, and its safeguards table marks Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) as not triggered. Its social impact matrix lists "Reubicación de 2 viviendas" — the relocation of two dwellings — between La Virginia and Ventana 1, rates the importance of that impact "Muy Baja", and sets against it a programme for relocating the affected dwellings; the text elsewhere says "Only two houses will be relocated (within their original plots)." Both are forward-looking. The matrix also gives 6.7 hectares needed for road widening, to be dealt with by easements, negotiated purchase or compensation for damage caused. The "desalojo" hit in the harvested material is the removal of temporary site installations, not an eviction. No completion report, evaluation review, resettlement plan or assessment report could be reached for this number, so no outcome document exists to check against the plan, and nothing found records anything actually done to anyone.

sibimbe-hydro-no-resettlement-triggered.drop_reason: Ecuador Hydro Sibimbe. Sibimbe is one of three run-of-river plants in the Netherlands Clean Development Facility umbrella appraisal of 16 December 2004, alongside Sabanilla and Abanico; the document's financing data sheet records the instrument as carbon financing and states "The project does not involve Bank financing", with emissions reductions purchases of 1.79 million euros for Sibimbe. The appraisal document says the project does not trigger the Involuntary Resettlement policy "since it will be sited in a rural, low density area". The passage carrying people — "A human settlement of about 10 families (perhaps the most consolidated settlement in the area of influence) is located 1.5 km from the penstock", with "Resettlement of no more than 4 families might be necessary" and "An Abbreviated Resettlement Plan will be prepared in case it is necessary" — sits in the impacts table for the intake, tunnel, penstock and power house on the Zamora, which is the Abanico sub-project and not Sibimbe. Every verb in it is conditional. The only other document for this number is a resettlement plan of February 2005, RP338, and the copy in the Bank's archive is a scan: the text route returns 357 bytes holding nothing but the disclosure stamp and the document number, so its contents could not be read. No completion report, evaluation review or assessment report could be reached.

uruguay-route-1-widening-titling-case.drop_reason: Uruguay Transport Infrastructure Maintenance and Rural Access. The outcome document harvested is the evaluation review of 1 May 2014; the completion report itself was not harvested, and the review is the route to it. The review carries the plan's figures with the plan's verb: "According to the Resettlement Plan, 11 families and 14 properties would be affected consisting of 11 housing units, 3 hangars, 1 commercial establishment, and a unit once used as a tire replacement shop." The same figures appear in the appraisal document of 26 April 2005 as "11 families are concerned and 14 properties will be affected", which is the plan-reprint trap the brief flags for this row. The review's statement of what actually happened is this: "The ICR reports (p. 9) that there were no major issues in dealing with the specific cases requiring resettlement. In widening National Route 1, in 2008 all of the affected properties were formally and properly handled with the exception of one property that faced titling problems." One property with a titling problem, with no count of people, no loss and no sum, is the whole of it, and the sentence that follows is attributed to the project team rather than to a document: "According to Project Team, the management of social and environmental issues was handled by the Borrower in a satisfactory manner with no significant issues arising in terms of safeguards." The project's own resettlement plan of March 2005 is in the archive as a scan whose text route returns only a cover page and a table of contents, so its census of affected persons could not be read.

uberaba-agua-viva-land-acquisitions.drop_reason: Brazil Municipal APL1: Uberaba. The completion report of 31 March 2014 says at paragraph 32 that the project documents indicate land acquisition would take place for the Component One works "to be financed with counterpart funds", that "The amount of land and value of transactions was small and the majority of the acquisitions had been carried out on a voluntary/amicable basis (through land donation, land swaps, and purchases at mutually agreed market prices)", and that the resettlement policy was not formally triggered at preparation. A portfolio review in January 2010 triggered it and the municipality prepared a retroactive involuntary resettlement action plan covering all the land acquisition that had happened since preparation. The report's conclusion on that: "Apart from the administrative time and effort in preparing and processing the necessary paperwork, there was no real impact of this retrofitting process on Project implementation." The retroactive plan was read. Its 2012 version says 18 areas had been acquired, four from legal entities and 14 from individuals, lists each by owner, and types them as vacant lots and areas of permanent preservation; its own argument is that the project gave value back to landlocked lots that had lost their market. Its table of affections shows one judicial expropriation, of part of the FAZU campus, where the expropriated party disputed the price and the case ended with a sentence issued and paid. The 2010 version says the areas needed "encontram-se totalmente desocupadas" — entirely unoccupied. No document found counts a household moved or a person who lost a home, a livelihood or a payment, and the evaluation review of 31 March 2015 adds only that not invoking the resettlement safeguard at appraisal was a shortcoming of quality at entry, which it rates Unsatisfactory.

limon-sewerage-drainage-resettlement-cas.drop_reason: Costa Rica Port-City of Limón Integrated Infrastructure Project. The completion report of 24 December 2014 is the outcome document and its resettlement paragraph reads in full: an abbreviated involuntary resettlement plan was developed during preparation "and to a large extent, adequately executed during the last phase of Project implementation. For the planned sewerage and drainage component, there were a total of 19 resettlement cases, 11 for sewerage and 8 for drainage, 18 of which were concluded by Project closure, and the remaining one in August 2014." That is a count of cases concluded, not of people or households relocated, and the verb attached to it is "concluded" rather than moved or resettled. No loss is recorded anywhere against those cases: no compensation withheld or paid below replacement cost, no livelihood not restored, no compulsion, no destination described. The project's resettlement plan of 9 June 2007 is a draft, marked BORRADOR, for families beside the Limoncito canal and the Limoncito wetland in the Barrios San Luis and Santa Fe; it budgets seven cases at 58,380,995 colones, about 112,108.79 dollars, and counts families to be affected in groups of nine, seven, four and three, all in the conditional. None of those figures is the report's 19, so the 19 is not a plan figure reprinted as a result; it is simply a count of cases with nothing attached. The report and the evaluation review of 24 June 2015 also differ on one safeguard policy: the report lists "Cultural and Physical Property (OP 11.03)" and the review lists "Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11)".

camalotales-water-tank-house-relocation.drop_reason: Honduras Rural Infrastructure Project. The one document with people in it is an abbreviated involuntary resettlement plan of 1 July 2014, RP314 V3, for the family of Don Valentín Romero in the community of Camalotales, Petoa, Santa Bárbara. It says that to build the distribution tank for the community water supply the relocation of his house is unavoidable, because hydraulic calculations and unstable ground rule out any other site, and that two related families are affected. It describes the family of five, three of them children, their subsistence farming and their present home, a one-room rustic wooden house with a dirt floor and an improvised latrine. It then records the agreement: his house would be rebuilt on a plot of his own seven metres away, where nothing else is affected, and he asked for no compensation for the plot. Every verb is forward-looking and the outcome it anticipates is a new house. The outcome documents were checked by name: the completion report of 26 December 2016 does not mention Camalotales, Petoa or Romero anywhere, and the evaluation review of 30 June 2017 says that "Though none of the project's interventions was expected to cause family displacements, an involuntary resettlement policy framework was prepared for the (unlikely) case of need for resettlement." No document found records the move happening, or any loss to anyone.

knollis-road-shop-removal-jamaica.drop_reason: Jamaica Inner City Basic Services for the Poor Project. Two abbreviated land acquisition and resettlement plans of 22 October 2013 cover Knollis, Bog Walk, St Catherine. One says the footprint of a planned football field and multipurpose building encroaches on a property to the east. The other says that resurfacing and realigning the Knollis road "will see the removal of a board structure that is used as a shop", describes the owner, his common-law wife and his student daughter, puts the shop's weekly earnings at 10,000 dollars and sets the compensation at 163,000 dollars in all: labour to remove the structure, dumping, 80,000 for materials to rebuild it, transport, labour to reconstruct and a week's income. It says the removal should not cause loss of stock, that the time taken may slightly affect earnings, that the decision to relocate had been made no more than three weeks before the plan was written, and that the owner "has expressed a willingness to relocate in order to facilitate the well needed development in the community". Both are forward-looking and neither records a loss incurred. The outcome documents go the other way. The completion report of 25 June 2014 and the field-based Project Performance Assessment Report of 1 April 2019 both say that the social investment fund "fully complied with the provisions of the Land Acquisition and Resettlement Policy Framework, successfully screening for cases of land acquisition and preparing abbreviated resettlement action plans acceptable to the Bank", and that all land transfers were properly documented, witnessed and held unencumbered titles. The assessment report's field work in the project communities records residents' accounts of better roads, mobility and electricity connections and no account of a loss. One plan says Knollis is in St Catherine and also that the upgrading works were approved by the Clarendon Parish Council.

buenos-aires-road-single-resettlement-ca.drop_reason: Argentina Buenos Aires Infrastructure Sustainable Investment Development Project, Phase II. The completion report of 14 June 2014 records one case and dismisses it: "the Involuntary Resettlement safeguard policy was triggered after the March 2011 MTR. According to preliminary sub-project designs, involuntary resettlement was not foreseen at the time of appraisal. However, a case of involuntary resettlement arose during the implementation of a road rehabilitation work due to a technical modification. This was, however, an isolated case. The PBA handled it satisfactorily and in compliance with OP 4.12 by applying the Resettlement Policy Framework (RPF) developed during the preparation of the APL1's AF." The evaluation review of 6 February 2015 reports the same single case in the same terms and says the province handled it in compliance with the policy. Neither document says how many people or households the case involved, where it was, what they lost or what they were paid. The one resettlement document harvested, of 1 August 2011, is the Marco de Política de Reasentamiento Involuntario, a policy framework; it sets out principles and procedures and carries no census, no site and no count. So the outcome document gives one unquantified case with no loss attached, and there is nothing to check it against.

sergipe-water-land-acquisitions.drop_reason: Brazil Sergipe Water. The completion report of 22 December 2020 says at paragraph 67 that the project "did not cause any involuntary resettlement of beneficiaries", that land acquisitions were needed for Component 3 works in the municipalities of Nossa Senhora de Dores and Itabaiana, that "The affected areas were partial portions of empty land, without houses/residences or other improvements, productive /commercial use or other livelihoods", and that "All areas were acquired and compensated before the beginning of the works and in compliance with OP 4.12." It records no non-compliance. The evaluation review of 11 June 2021 repeats it. The one harm-shaped sentence in the report is about other people's occupations, not the project's doing: it says the social action plan succeeded but "it was not possible to prevent the advance of irregular occupations around the dams, which may in the future compromise water quality and also a risk to occupants in areas close to the dams reservoirs" — a risk in the future, to people who moved in of their own accord. The project's resettlement framework of 26 October 2010 was read for the counts it carries, and they are of settlements that already existed: two irregular settlements next to an irrigation perimeter, Fazenda Tingui with 366 families and Mario Lago with 96, and the community of Tabua with 28 families occupying a legal reserve inside the perimeter. The framework says there is pressure from organised social movements to restructure the perimeter, that it is not possible to resettle all these families inside it, and that the agrarian reform institute was working on a strategy and a resettlement plan for the problem. None of that is displacement by this project, and the outcome document says the project caused none.

champ-de-mars-solar-lighting-fatality.drop_reason: Haiti Rebuilding Energy Infrastructure and Access. The completion report of 29 July 2021 says at paragraph 96 that "The project required no physical or economic displacement." Two incidents in the outcome documents were checked. A fatality: paragraph 99 says the Bank was informed of "a fatality of a member of the contractor's team installing solar lighting on the Champ de Mars which had occurred in August 2019 during the 'Peyi Lock' period when civil disturbances led to many casualties", that the Bank team was concerned at the long delay in reporting it and documented it through the Environment and Social Incident Response Toolkit, and that "The team's assessment was that the incident was not project-related, but rather a direct consequence of civil unrest, and that the contractor had undertaken mitigation measures to the extent possible under the circumstances." So the only document that gives a cause for the death gives a cause outside the works, which leaves the death uncounted under the project's rule and leaves nothing else attached to it: no name, no compensation question, no finding against anyone. An allegation: paragraph 98 says a rumour of a possible gender-based violence case related to the Drouet micro-hydroelectric rehabilitation sub-project was reported by project counterparts, that "the Bank's management decided not to take action because the alleged incident could not be confirmed", and that the episode led the Bank to strengthen prevention and mitigation measures across its Haitian energy portfolio. An unconfirmed rumour is not a documented harm. The safeguards count is Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) and Safety of Dams (OP/BP 4.37), with a framework and a resettlement policy framework disclosed before appraisal.

p105959-already-on-map.note: The dedupe script reports P105959 on the map as pinheiros-station-collapse-sao-paulo, confirmed by place and years: that case is built on the same document as the one document harvested here, the resettlement plan of December 2007 for the Pinheiros station accident, disclosed as RP591 under the Line 4 additional financing, and it already carries the plan's property, household and death figures, the São Paulo state court improbity judgment of 16 February 2024, and the finding that the additional financing was approved fifteen months after the collapse and so did not pay for the works that collapsed. Nothing in the harvested document adds to it.
